Getty Images filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on Wednesday, formalizing restructuring plans unveiled more than a week ago as part of its move to go private.

Getty said the affiliates of the Getty family and Koch Equity Development, which committed to provide up to $533 million in new equity, will own 100% of the company after the restructuring.
Getty said on Wednesday it launched a solicitation process to secure formal approval for its reorganization plan announced last week.
The visual-content provider said it will continue operating in the ordinary course throughout the process, with no impact on content contributors, partners, customers, employees or vendors.
Getty Images expects to complete the restructuring by year-end.
In a filing at the Delaware bankruptcy court, the company listed both estimated assets and liabilities in the range of $1 billion to $10 billion.
Getty, which competes with Reuters and the Associated Press in providing photos and videos for editorial use, said financing from Koch Equity Development of up to $143 million would support the restructuring process.

Getty Images Holdings reaches deal with lenders, shareholders and noteholders to take company private and wipe out warrant litigation claims through Chapter 11 – Legal Analysis
- USD 533m new equity investment from Getty Family Entities and KED
- Prepackaged Chapter 11 case planned with USD 143m DIP loan from KED
- Plan distributions include accrued interest, new notes, and USD 170.2m unsecured noteholder recovery
Getty Images announced on 12 October that it entered into a restructuring support agreement (RSA) that would take the global visual content creator and marketplace private, with certain Getty Family Entities,[1] through certain of their affiliated entities, and affiliates of Koch Equity Development (KED), owning 100% of the company upon emergence from a prepackaged Chapter 11 case.
Under the agreement, members of the Getty family and KED, as consenting shareholders, agreed to invest up to USD 533m of new equity.
However, the ECL provides that KED will not be obligated to contribute cash exceeding approximately USD 158.2m, and Getty Family Entities’ obligations will be capped at USD 162m.
Funded debt holders are also RSA parties.
Holders of 83.5% of the company’s unsecured bonds have agreed to retire USD 270m of outstanding senior unsecured notes, and holders of approximately 89% of the company’s secured bonds and term loans, and 100% of revolving credit facility lenders will reduce interest obligations and extend maturities on Getty’s secured debt.
Getty plans to implement these transactions through a plan of reorganization.
It will commence Chapter 11 cases for certain of the company’s US entities and begin soliciting plan votes in the coming days.
It will then commence a prepackaged Chapter 11 case in the coming weeks.
According to the company, the requisite majority of creditors have agreed to vote to accept the plan.
Postpetition financing and exit capital structure
The cases will be funded with a USD 143m DIP loan provided by KED and/or its affiliates to Getty Images Holdings, as borrower.
The other Chapter 11 debtors will guarantee the DIP loans, which will bear PIK interest at Term SOFR + 5%.
On the plan’s effective date, the DIP loans will be deemed equity infusions and treated as interests in the reorganized Getty Images (New Interests).
The RSA provides that consenting shareholders will make approximately USD 433.2m in equity investments (minus the amount of the DIP loans).
To the extent any of the USD 30m delayed-draw DIP loans are outstanding on the restructuring effective date, KED will (and will cause its affiliates to) contribute, exchange, surrender, equitize, and discharge such claims in exchange for 100% of new preferred interests.
In terms of the reorganized entities’ capital structure, JPMorgan Chase Bank will be the administrative agent on an exit credit agreement, with the amounts borrowed under that agreement dependent on plan distributions, discussed below.
Also, the applicable reorganized company party, referred to as the “New Issuer”[2] will issue USD 580m in new notes due April 2032.
Interest on those notes will be determined as follows:
Source: Restructuring Support Agreement
The New Issuer will also issue EUR 313.9m in new EUR term loans due April 2032, with interest to be calculated as follows
Source: Restructuring Support Agreement
In addition, the New Borrower will enter into a new USD 150m revolving credit facility that will mature in January 2031.
Interest rates under that facility will be set as follows:
Source: Restructuring Support Agreement
Distributions on prepetition claims
In terms of plan distributions, Getty has grouped USD and EUR term loan lenders and secured noteholders in a single class.
The plan will generally propose that accrued interest be paid in full, in cash, with differing treatments for the principal portion of the secured claims.
Holders of the 11.25% secured notes and USD term loans will receive new notes in an equal principal amount.
However, USD term loan lenders that do not consent to receive new notes, will instead receive USD term loans on terms to be negotiated among the company RSA parties, consenting shareholders, and required consenting secured lenders.
Holders of the EUR term loans, on account of the principal amount of their claims, will receive new EUR term loans in an equal principal amount except that consenting shareholders, such as KED, will receive their pro rata share of interests in the new Getty Images (New Interests) in accordance with a “Final Allocation Schedule,” to be filed with the bankruptcy court and subject to up to 10% dilution under the management incentive plan (MIP).
Unsecured noteholders will receive their pro rata share of approximately USD 170.2m (Unsecured Notes Recovery) and the debtors will pay up to USD 200,000 of the trustee’s fees and expenses.
Revolver lenders will receive accrued interest in full, in cash and their pro rata share of new revolving loans for principal.
General unsecured creditors will not be entitled to vote on the plan as their claims will be left unimpaired.
Holders of equity interests will be wiped out and shareholders will be deemed to reject the plan.
Getty also plans to use Chapter 11 to wipe out a USD 62.5m state court judgment entered against it on 25 September.
In July 2024, Funicular Funds and other plaintiffs sued Getty asserting that it failed to permit the conversion of warrants into publicly traded shares, while transferring that value to Getty and its insiders.
The warrants were issued through the 2020 initial public offering of an affiliated special purpose acquisition company.
The largest awards granted through the judgment, inclusive of interest were USD 11.9m to Highbridge Tactical Credit Master Fund, USD 10.7m to PW Aero, and USD 7.7m to Highbridge SPAC Opportunity Fund.
Over two dozen plaintiffs received awards under the judgment.
Getty has since appealed.
Section 510(b) of the Bankruptcy Code generally subordinates certain claims arising from the purchase or sale of securities.
According to Getty, the plaintiffs’ claims are therefore entitled to the same priority as shareholders and will not receive any distribution under the plan.
Reducing claims subject to section 510(b) of the Bankruptcy Code to a judgment does not alter their subordination under section 510(b).
Additional plan provisions
The plan will provide typical non-debtor releases, covering the parties to the RSA, US Bank Trust Company as trustee and collateral agent on the prepetition secured notes, JPMorgan Chase Bank as agent on the prepetition credit agreement, and the DIP agent.which has yet to be identified.

Defense Intelligence Agency, believes that a shared concern by both parties regarding the threat posed by China serves as a foundation for policy continuity.
“While there's never unanimous positions on every single issue about China, there certainly is a very strong bipartisan trend within the House as well as the Senate when it comes to the threats represented by China,” he said in a pre-election interview with VOA.
Shedd predicts that the president will continue to seek constructive engagement with China, while Congress will keep scrutinizing security threats.
On Wednesday, China Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning said that Beijing is ready to continue working with Washington.
In response to a question at the regular press briefing, she described the U.S.
midterm elections as “a domestic affair” and stated that “China stands ready to continue working with the U.S.
to uphold and deliver on the important common understandings reached by the two heads of state.”
Room for maneuvering
Experts are assessing how the midterm election results could affect the Trump administration’s ability to deal with China.
Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for the Asia-Pacific region at the French investment bank Natixis, told Reuters, that the newly empowered Democrats could try to limit Trump's maneuvering power.
"Democrats are unlikely to give Trump free rein on deals with Beijing," she said.
However, Jon Czin, a fellow at the Brookings Institution and former director for China affairs at the White House National Security Council, says when it comes to Washington’s China policy directions, while Congress may exert greater pressure and advance relevant bills, it is the president who remains in the driver’s seat.
"I don't think there will be big fluctuations in U.S.-China policy." said Czin in a pre-election interview with VOA.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that he learned as a former U.S.
senator that a new Congress cannot change foreign policies that the president was elected to carry out.
“To my great frustration, when I was a member of the Senate, I realized that while there are things we could do, ultimately the foreign policy decisions are made by the Executive Branch,” Rubio said last Friday.
“Congress plays a role.
There’s no doubt about it.
But the central role belongs to the Executive Branch.”
After Tuesday’s midterm elections, President Trump has emphasized "one of the stronger powers that a President has" — veto power.
VOA Mandarin’s Yu-wen Cheng and Lin Feng contributed to this report.

US President Donald Trump will travel to China from March 31 to April 2, a White House official said on Friday, setting dates for a highly anticipated encounter amid tension between the world's biggest economies.
Trump is expected to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping as part of the extended visit, as the two sides weigh whether to extend a trade truce that paused a tariffs escalation, said the official, who declined to be named while discussing details that have not been publicly announced.

The visit would be the leaders' first talks since February and their first in-person visit since an October meeting in South Korea, where Trump agreed to trim tariffs on China in exchange for Beijing cracking down on the illicit fentanyl trade, resuming US soybean purchases and keeping rare earths exports flowing.
While the October meeting largely sidestepped the sensitive issue of Taiwan, in February, Xi raised US arms sales to the island.

China confirms discussions underway on historic Xi-Trump-Putin meeting
Summary
Beijing confirmed discussions with relevant parties about a possible meeting between Chinese leader Xi Jinping, U.S.
President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, potentially this month in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the APEC summit.
No meeting or agenda has been finalized.
Experts said the gathering could be largely a photo opportunity, with the leaders’ interests at odds and China seeking to manage the optics and costs.
Trump has expressed interest in discussing nuclear arms control, while Putin is focused on Ukraine.
Key Facts
- Mao Ning, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson, said China was communicating with relevant parties about a meeting of the three leaders.
- The APEC grouping has 21 members, including the United States and Russia, and China is hosting this year’s leaders summit.
- Trump is expected to meet Xi in Shenzhen for the third time this year, while the existing trade truce is set to expire in January.
- U.S.
Trade Representative Jamieson Greer urged Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng to take concrete steps on agricultural purchases, rare earths and other critical minerals.
- Xinhua said China raised concerns during the call about Washington’s restrictive economic and trade measures against Beijing.
WASHINGTON — Beijing has confirmed for the first time that it is discussing a historic meeting between Chinese leader Xi Jinping, U.S.
President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Mao Ning, a spokesperson for the Chinese foreign ministry, said at a press briefing this week in Beijing that China “is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state.” Nothing is set, but the three-leader gathering would take place this month on the sidelines of a regional summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen.
If it happens, it would be historic.
Experts, however, say the three leaders are unlikely to discuss anything substantive because their interests are at odds , but they would gather for a photo, with China carefully choreographing the meeting.
“I think it will happen.
The question is the format and the content,” said Sun Yun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center.
“China wants the image but not the costs.”
Beijing is the host of this year’s leaders summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a 21-member grouping that includes the U.S.
and Russia.
Trump is expected to travel to Shenzhen to meet Xi for the third time this year, maintaining a fragile trade truce that is set to expire in January.
In a sign that tensions persist, U.S.
Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in a Friday video call with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng urged Beijing to take “concrete actions to fully implement its past commitments, particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases , rare earths, and other critical minerals ,” according to a statement from Greer's office.
China's official news agency Xinhua reported Saturday that both sides had in-depth and constructive exchanges in the call, and that China expressed concerns about Washington’s restrictive economic and trade measures against Beijing.
While he’s in China, Trump has said he would be interested in meeting Xi and Putin to discuss nuclear arms controls, though Putin is focused on talking about the war in Ukraine without Kyiv at the table.
“Putin has the most to gain from a leaders’ trilateral, and the Russians are clearly behind the push for a meeting, which would be a diplomatic coup,” said Danny Russel, a former senior State Department official who served in former President Barack Obama’s administration.
Trump, with his “crush on authoritarian strongmen," would love the meeting, though he clearly has been warned by his advisers to steer clear of Ukraine as a topic of the discussions, said Russel, who is now a distinguished fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
Sun of the Stimson Center said Russia would likely use the summit to nudge China and the U.S.
closer to Moscow's positions on Ukraine, while “China will have to manage Russian manipulation.”
China also would not engage in talks on arms controls or discussions about Ukraine or Iran, other than its diplomatic refrain that peace is important and wars should end, Sun said.
Beijing's biggest challenge may be the perception.
The summit “should not be equated to three great powers dividing up the world,” she said.
The meeting may amount to no more than a photo opportunity that would allow Putin to be seen next to U.S.
and Chinese leaders, said Craig Singleton, senior director of the China program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.
“But these photo opportunities have diminishing diplomatic returns,” Singleton said.
“The spectacle may be historic without producing anything particularly consequential.”

US President Donald Trump will fly to Manila on November 16 for the ASEAN Summit, the White House has confirmed, before continuing to China for a separate leaders’ meeting.
It would be Trump’s first trip to the Philippines since he attended the 2017 ASEAN Summit.
What the White House confirmed
The White House told the New York Post that Trump will take part in the ASEAN Summit in Manila on November 16, then head to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit from November 17 to 19.
The report was carried and repeated by other outlets, including OrissaPOST and Indian wire aggregators.
A White House official said the goal of the trip is to demonstrate America’s commitment to its allies in Southeast Asia and to advance US economic and national security objectives.
Rumors that Trump would attend had circulated for weeks.
Malacañang confirms the visit
Malacañang confirmed on Wednesday, October 14, that Trump will attend the summit, putting the host government on record after weeks of speculation.
Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said at a press briefing that the visit is set.
“It is confirmed, but the details will not come from me,” she said.
Asked whether Trump’s visit is connected to the signing of the Pax Silica framework, Castro did not answer.
The 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits run from November 16 to 18 at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City, the same dates Marcos declared special non-working days in Metro Manila.
Until the Palace confirmation on October 14, Philippine officials had only said Manila was still waiting for word.
Philippine Ambassador to the United States Jose Manuel Romualdez said in September that the country was “awaiting confirmation” on whether Trump would make the trip.
Why the Manila stop matters
The Philippines is chairing ASEAN in 2026 and will host the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits in Manila on November 16 to 18.
The main venue is the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City, which the Palace has prepared for the event.
Malacañang earlier declared November 16 to 18 special non-working days in Metro Manila, in a Palace declaration that clears the way for the summit’s security and traffic arrangements.
The meeting runs under the theme “Navigating Our Future, Together.” Hosting deliverables include an ASEAN-China Code of Conduct in the South China Sea, an ASEAN Centre on Maritime Studies in Manila, a Digital Economy Framework, and promotion of the so-called “silver economy,” according to the Manila Times.
A busy Asia swing for Trump
The Shenzhen leg would be Trump’s third in-person meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this year, after Xi’s state visit to the White House in September and their sit-down in Beijing in May.
The two are also expected to meet at the G20 summit in Miami in December.
During Xi’s White House visit, Washington and Beijing announced an artificial intelligence alert system and extended their trade truce to January 10, 2027, buying more time for negotiations.
Manila has tracked that thaw closely because it shapes the West Philippine Sea policy space for the Philippines.
Trump’s last official Philippine trip was the 2017 ASEAN Summit.
Last year he attended the ASEAN Summit in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, and the APEC meeting in Gyeongju, South Korea.
Key facts
| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Manila event | 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits, Nov.
16 to 18, 2026 |
| Trump’s Manila date | November 16, 2026 |
| Main venue | Philippine International Convention Center, Pasay City |
| Next stop | APEC Summit, Shenzhen, China, Nov.
17 to 19, 2026 |
| Summit theme | “Navigating Our Future, Together” |
| Metro Manila | Nov.
16 to 18 declared special non-working days |
| Trump’s last PH visit | 2017 ASEAN Summit |
What to watch
The summit is expected to draw other leaders, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.
For Manila, the stakes are both diplomatic and economic as it tries to press a binding Code of Conduct in the South China Sea while balancing ties with Washington and Beijing.
The Philippine leg also carries a domestic logistics load.
Hosting a US presidential visit alongside the ASEAN leaders’ meetings means tighter security, road closures, and a heavier bill for the host government, all concentrated in the capital region.
The confirmation ends months of speculation that began after Secretary of State Marco Rubio signalled the president’s interest during ASEAN foreign ministers’ meetings in Manila in July.
Marcos has been inviting Trump to visit, and has also renewed an invitation to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi for the ASEAN-India Summit and the East Asia Summit.

at the White House on July 22, 2025.

What is Bitcoin?
Bitcoin is the first cryptocurrency ever created and is still the most widely recognized digital coin available in 2026.
Its market capitalization sits around $1.33 trillion, far above runner-up Ethereum, which has a market value of roughly $233 billion.
At its core, Bitcoin is a decentralized digital currency.
That means it operates on a peer-to-peer network instead of being controlled by a government, bank, or other central authority.
It lets you transfer value straight to another person without using a financial middleman.
Many investors are drawn to Bitcoin because they see it as a potential hedge against inflation or simply as a way to add another asset class to their portfolio.
Over the past decade, its performance has been massive, often beating the returns of major stock market indices, which helps explain why it has captured so much attention.
However, like other cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin is exposed to extreme volatility and can experience rapid price swings.
Bitcoin price history
Since launching in 2009, Bitcoin’s journey has been anything but smooth.
In the early days, software developer and early believer Laszlo Hanyecz famously spent 10,000 Bitcoins on a couple of pizzas; at the time of this writing, those coins would be worth more than $668 million.
Over roughly the last decade, Bitcoin’s price has soared by more than 15,000%.
That upside has come with serious risk, as cryptocurrencies tend to be highly unpredictable.
Bitcoin has experienced steep drops, at times losing tens of thousands of dollars in value within a few months, but it has also staged similarly dramatic rallies.
In 2025, it ended the calendar year about 30% below the all-time high it hit in October of that same year.
What affects Bitcoin’s price?
Several forces can influence the price of Bitcoin, including:
- Investor speculation: As with many assets, trader sentiment and hype play a major role in Bitcoin’s value.
In the short term, its demand often reflects investor instincts and speculative trading activity rather than deeper fundamentals.
- Adoption by major companies: As businesses adopt crypto technology and begin accepting Bitcoin as payment, its growth potential can increase.
For instance, Bitcoin’s price climbed following announcements from companies like Tesla and Ferrari that they would accept it for certain purchases.
- Economy: Bitcoin doesn’t react to inflation data or Federal Reserve decisions in quite the same way as traditional investments such as stocks.
Even so, it often performs better when the U.S.
economy is strong.
When consumers feel flush, they may be more willing to experiment with alternatives like crypto.
- Regulatory developments: Cryptocurrency is still a relatively young space, and regulation is evolving.
New rules or government actions can make investors nervous and affect Bitcoin’s price.
How to buy and invest in Bitcoin
You have several ways to gain exposure to Bitcoin.
Here are some of the most common.
Buy Bitcoin on a cryptocurrency exchange
One of the most straightforward strategies is to buy Bitcoin directly.
You can open an account with a cryptocurrency exchange, connect it to your bank account, and then use your funds to purchase Bitcoin.
Invest in Bitcoin ETFs
If you prefer not to hold Bitcoin yourself, you might consider a cryptocurrency exchange-traded fund (ETF).
A Bitcoin ETF owns Bitcoin on your behalf, and its shares trade on regular stock exchanges.
This approach lets you avoid setting up a separate crypto wallet and lowers the risk of losing access to your coins due to password or wallet mishaps.
Buy crypto stocks
Investors who are hesitant to invest in Bitcoin directly can also look at stocks tied to the crypto industry.
These may include technology companies, publicly traded crypto exchanges, or payment processors.
Because these businesses use or hold Bitcoin in their operations, their performance can be influenced by Bitcoin’s price, giving you indirect exposure.
Open a Bitcoin IRA
For those focused on retirement, a Bitcoin IRA might be appealing.
It’s a tax-advantaged retirement account that lets you use your retirement contributions to buy Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies.
A Bitcoin IRA offers the same tax benefits and contribution limits as traditional or Roth IRAs, but it allows you to invest in alternative assets.
Bitcoin vs.
other cryptocurrencies
While Bitcoin is the best-known name in crypto, it’s not your only choice.
As you decide where to allocate your money, you may also want to look at:
- Ethereum: Ethereum is the second-largest cryptocurrency after Bitcoin.
Unlike Bitcoin, it wasn’t created mainly as a currency; instead, it was built as a decentralized computing platform and is widely used by developers.
- Tether: Tether is a type of stablecoin, which means its value is tied to another asset.
In this case, it’s linked to the U.S.
dollar.
Because of that, Tether usually experiences less volatility than Bitcoin, but it doesn’t offer the same potential upside.
- XRP: XRP is designed specifically for transferring money across borders quickly and at low cost.

Is it a good time to invest in Bitcoin?
Compared with established blue-chip stocks like Walmart, Procter & Gamble, and Coca-Cola, Bitcoin is still a relatively new asset.
That makes it difficult to predict how it will behave over several decades.
Even so, its performance in recent years has been extraordinary.
And its price may continue to rise as more companies decide to take Bitcoin as a form of payment.
As it matures, its price swings could become less dramatic.
As with any investment, it’s important to not go all in.
Only put money into Bitcoin that you won’t need in the near future, and make sure the rest of your portfolio is diversified enough so other holdings can help offset Bitcoin’s volatility.
In practical terms, Bitcoin often makes the most sense as a long-term holding rather than a short-term trade, and it may not be a fit for investors who are easily rattled by big price moves.
If you’re prepared to hold for years and keep it as one slice of a broader, well-balanced portfolio, putting some money into Bitcoin could be a reasonable choice.

How much will Bitcoin be worth in 2030?
While the answer is obviously unknowable, crypto experts are generally optimistic about the short-term success of Bitcoin.
Some models price it at more than $700,000 by 2030, with conservative estimates closer to $300,000.

polymarket-6967620.text:
Bitcoin prices dropped below $69,000 on Friday marking a significant decline as more than $1.41 billion in cryptocurrency futures positions were liquidated within 24 hours.
The market, which has seen its total capitalization plunge from levels seen in early October to roughly $1.4 trillion as of mid-November, faces pressure from shrinking stablecoin liquidity and negative outflows from spot Bitcoin ETFs.
The downturn pushed Bitcoin to its lowest levels since August 19, 2026.
This sell-off was exacerbated by the forced unwinding of leveraged positions, with CoinGlass data showing that 185,172 traders were impacted by the volatility.
Long positions—bets that the price would rise—accounted for approximately 89.5% to 95.3% of the total liquidated volume, according to reporting on market activity.
The largest single order was a $31.09 million Bitcoin long on the Hyperliquid exchange, which was closed at $72,250 as the asset began its slide.
Jiang Zhuoer, who identified the next support level at $69,100, said that the asset had fallen below the 50% Fibonacci retracement level of its previous rally at $72,600.
US-listed spot Bitcoin ETFs have recorded $1.44 billion in withdrawals over five consecutive sessions, according to recent market analysis.
This turn in sentiment has left these funds in the red for 2026, with $1.56 billion in net outflows recorded.
This is a stark reversal from previous years; funds saw $21.37 billion in net inflows during 2025 and $35.24 billion in 2024.
The supply of major stablecoins has decreased by $14.2 billion over 30 days, depriving the market of the capital needed to absorb selling pressure.
Weakness in technology stocks has reinforced the broader de-risking move, and once Bitcoin lost the $72,000-$73,000 area, forced liquidations accelerated the decline.
Zhang stated
The financial environment remains sensitive to interest rate expectations.
Following stronger-than-expected October inflation data, traders have priced in an approximately 80% chance of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December.
This shift has bolstered the US Dollar Index, which traded above 103, its highest level since April 2025.
Rising rates increase the cost of holding non-interest-paying assets like Bitcoin, according to sector analysis.
The Crypto Fear & Greed Index plummeted to 20 on November 13, indicating "Extreme Fear" among market participants.
Institutional trading platform Talos reported in its weekly analysis that order-book depth across Binance, Kraken, and Coinbase dropped to $72 million on November 9, roughly 33% below normal levels.

polymarket-6967620.text:
The crypto market ended Thursday night with its steepest daily loss in weeks.
At 07:30 UTC on November 13, 2026, bitcoin traded at about $69,000, down a little over 6% in 24 hours, after touching an intraday low of $67,922 according to CoinGecko.
Total crypto market capitalization fell about 7% over the same period to roughly $2.35 trillion.
If you are asking why is crypto down today, our running explainer tracks every sell-off of the year.
This crypto news roundup sets out what is driving the move: forced selling of leveraged positions, outflows from US spot bitcoin ETFs, a strong dollar with rising Treasury yields, and thin order books.
Our first report with key price levels is Bitcoin price falls below $70,000.
Crypto news at a glance: bitcoin, ether, BNB and XRP this morning
Losses run through the large caps, but not evenly.
As of 07:30 UTC, per CoinGecko data:
- Bitcoin: about $69,000, down 6.2% in 24 hours.
- Ether: about $1,942, down 5.2%.
According to CoinDesk, ether fell below $2,000 for the first time since August; see Ethereum price below $2,000.
- BNB: about $634, down 5.9%; more in BNB falls below $650.
- Solana: about $80.50, down 2.9%.
- XRP: about $1.03, down 1.3%, with an intraday low just under $1.
XRP and Solana fell less than bitcoin and ether over the past day, but both had already lost more earlier in the week: over seven days XRP is down a little over 14% and Solana just over 10%, per CoinGecko.
For medium-term scenarios, see our bitcoin price prediction and ethereum price prediction.
Liquidations: more than $1.3 billion in leveraged bets wiped out in 24 hours
A liquidation is the forced closing of a leveraged position by an exchange once the posted collateral no longer covers it.
Based on CoinGlass data analysed by CoinDesk early Friday, more than $1.3 billion in crypto futures were liquidated within 24 hours, about $677 million of them on bitcoin.
The largest single liquidation was a long bitcoin position worth more than $31 million on Hyperliquid, according to the same report.
Because CoinGlass uses a rolling 24-hour window, totals depend on when they are captured.
Later snapshots reported by KuCoin News and Bloomingbit reached up to $1.62 billion.
The defensible range is therefore $1.3 billion to $1.6 billion, most of it from traders who had bet on rising prices.
Bitcoin ETF outflows: why US funds are weighing on the price
The second driver is US fund flows.
According to Cointelegraph, BlackRock's IBIT recorded more than $2 billion in net outflows over nine consecutive sessions through Wednesday.
Across all US spot bitcoin ETFs, nearly $1.44 billion left over five sessions.
Preliminary Farside data showed a further $47.7 million in net outflows on Thursday, with BlackRock and Fidelity figures still pending.
A spot ETF holds actual bitcoin as backing.
When investors redeem shares, the fund generally has to sell bitcoin, which adds to the pressure from liquidations.
Dollar and Treasury yields: the macro pressure on crypto
CoinDesk points to a strong US dollar: the Dollar Index rose above 103, its highest since April 2025.
After a hotter-than-expected October CPI reading, markets also raised the odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December.
Per Cointelegraph, data from 10x Research show bitcoin fell 5.9% between November 5 and 12, while the 10-year Treasury yield climbed above 5%.
Order book depth: why the bitcoin price swings so hard
Order book depth measures how many buy and sell orders sit close to the current price.
The thinner it is, the further a large sale moves the market.
According to Talos, cited by Cointelegraph, bitcoin order book depth across major exchanges stood at $72 million on November 9, roughly 33% below normal.
Talos senior research associate Tanay Ved said liquidity remains thin while leverage stays elevated, leaving the market vulnerable to sharp moves in either direction.
Fear and Greed Index at 20: extreme fear in the crypto market
Sentiment matches the price action.
The Crypto Fear and Greed Index from alternative.me reads 20 on Friday, which is "Extreme Fear", down from 28 the day before.
Cointelegraph notes this is the lowest reading since July 8.
How the market behaved after earlier spells of extreme fear is covered in our Fear and Greed Index history.
A low reading describes the mood; on its own it does not predict whether prices fall further or turn.

In short
Bitcoin fell below $75,000 on 6 November 2026 and traded near $71,600 on 12 November [3][4].
US spot bitcoin ETFs lost a net $1.28 billion in the week to 6 November, the most since late June [1][2].
Reports link the fall to rate-hike expectations, a technology-stock selloff and weak institutional demand [3][10].
Key takeaways
- Bitcoin dropped below $75,000 on Friday 6 November 2026 for the first time since August, according to Dow Jones [3], and fell as low as about $71,200 on 12 November, a near 12-week low [4].
- US spot bitcoin ETFs had net outflows of $1,281.7 million from 2 to 6 November, by Farside Investors' daily data [1]; CoinDesk, citing SoSoValue, called it the largest weekly outflow since the week of 22 to 28 June [2].
- Outflows continued: $1.44 billion left over the five trading days from 5 to 11 November, and about $1.88 billion in November to 11 November [1][5].
- October consumer prices rose 0.4% (core 0.3%), more than expected, which Reuters said cemented expectations of a Federal Reserve rate rise in December [9][10].
- Strategy's average bitcoin cost was $75,456 per coin as of 8 November 2026 [7]; the widely quoted $76,052 figure dates from 1 February 2026 [8].
- This is general information, not financial advice.
Prices are a dated snapshot as of 13 November 2026.
How far has bitcoin fallen in November 2026?
Bitcoin, the largest cryptocurrency, slipped below the round $75,000 mark on Friday 6 November 2026, its first time under that level since August, according to Dow Jones Newswires [3].
It fell about 5% on Thursday 5 November, as US technology stocks sold off heavily that week [3]; Decrypt dates a 5.5% fall in the Nasdaq Composite to 5 November [5].
On Monday 9 November it was trading around $74,162 [3].
The slide deepened later in the week.
On Thursday 12 November bitcoin traded as low as about $71,200, its lowest level in nearly 12 weeks, and was down 3.4% at about $71,600 when The Block published its report [4].
Ethereum, Solana and XRP also fell more than 3.5% over the same 24 hours [4].
More than $750 million of leveraged crypto positions were liquidated in that period, over $634 million of them bets on rising prices, according to CoinGlass data cited by The Block [4].
A liquidation is the forced closing of a borrowed position when the trader's collateral runs out.
These are snapshots.
Bitcoin trades around the clock on many exchanges, so a price quoted without a time and a source can be wrong within minutes.
This guide gives each figure with its date and its source, and none of them is a forecast.
For the basics of how bitcoin works, how new coins are created and why its supply is capped, see the guide What Is Bitcoin?
on this site.
What are bitcoin ETF outflows, and how big were they?
A spot bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF) is a fund listed on a stock exchange that holds bitcoin itself, so investors can buy exposure through an ordinary brokerage account.
The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) approved the listing of the several spot bitcoin exchange-traded products on 10 January 2024 [13].
The SEC chair stressed at the time that the approval did not approve or endorse bitcoin, which he called primarily a speculative, volatile asset [13].
An outflow means that, across a day or a week, investors took more money out of these funds than they put in.
Analysts watch the figure because the funds are seen as a proxy for institutional demand [2].
The week of 2 to 6 November
Farside Investors, which publishes daily flow data for each US spot bitcoin ETF, recorded net flows of minus $398.6 million on 2 November, minus $115.6 million on 3 November, plus $74.6 million on 4 November, minus $430.2 million on 5 November and minus $411.9 million on 6 November [1].
That adds up to a net outflow of $1,281.7 million for the week [1].
CoinDesk, using data from SoSoValue, gave the same total of $1.282 billion and said it was the largest weekly outflow since the week of 22 to 28 June [2].
Four of the five trading days were negative [2].
The selling was concentrated in one fund.
BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) had net outflows on all five days, totalling about $1.21 billion, while Fidelity's FBTC had net inflows on 3, 4 and 6 November, by Farside's table [1].
After 6 November
Outflows did not stop.
Farside's data shows minus $201.0 million on 9 November, minus $95.0 million on 10 November and minus $299.8 million on 11 November [1].

When Decrypt reported on 12 November, the funds' total net assets had fallen to $93.7 billion, about 45% below their October 2025 peak of $169.5 billion, as both outflows and lower prices reduced them [5].
Why did the bitcoin price fall?
No single cause has been proven.
The reports describe several pressures that arrived together.
They are listed here as reported explanations.
1.
Expectations of higher US interest rates
Higher interest rates tend to weigh on assets that pay no yield, such as cryptocurrencies, Dow Jones noted [3].
Dow Jones reported that stronger-than-expected US jobs data on Friday 6 November raised expectations that the Federal Reserve would raise rates [3].
The October consumer price index (CPI), published on 10 November, then showed prices up 0.4% in a month and core prices, which exclude food and energy, up 0.3% [9].
Reuters reported that both figures were above economists' forecasts and that the report cemented expectations of a rate rise in December [10].
Markets were pricing a roughly 89% chance of a quarter-point rise at the December meeting, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool as cited by Reuters [10].
2.

US technology stocks fell heavily in the week of 5 November, and bitcoin followed [3].
Decrypt reported that on 5 November, the day the Nasdaq Composite fell about 5.5%, bitcoin ETFs had net outflows of about $430 million [5].
On 12 November The Block linked a further drop to the abrupt resignation of Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang [4].
The selloff in chip and AI stocks is covered in a separate guide on why chip and AI stocks plunged on 5 November 2026.
3.
Weak demand from new buyers
Analysts quoted by Decrypt said the bigger worry was a shortage of new buyers.
BitGo's head of research said the supply of dollar-pegged stablecoins shrank 1.9% to $286.3 billion, suggesting little fresh capital was waiting to enter [5].
He also said a hedge-fund strategy known as the basis trade, which bought ETF shares while selling futures, had become less attractive, prompting many funds to exit [5].
Stablecoins such as USDT are explained in the guide What Is USDT?

4.
Industry-specific worries
Dow Jones reported that the sector had endured a difficult 10 days after a $6.3 billion hack of the crypto exchange Binance, and that some investors feared the Democratic election gains could bring greater scrutiny of the crypto industry [3].
These are investor fears as reported, not measured effects.
Is bitcoin below Strategy's cost basis?
Strategy is a US company that holds bitcoin as a corporate treasury asset [12].
Its cost basis, the average price it paid per coin, is a reference point for whether its holding is above or below what it paid.

spot bitcoin ETFs logged $1.28 billion in net outflows last week, their worst week since late June, per The Block's analysis of SoSoValue data.
It was the funds' second straight negative week and made the top ten largest weekly outflows since they launched in January 2024 at #7.
The funds saw outflows every day except Wednesday last week, per the data.
They lost $398.6 million on Monday, $115.6 million on Tuesday, $430.2 million on Thursday and $411.9 million on Friday, with Wednesday's relatively modest $74.6 million inflow marking the only positive day.

Bitcoin funds turn negative for 2026
The week's outflows erased bitcoin ETFs' gains for the year.

Monday's outflows pushed that figure below zero, and the funds closed Friday at about $914.1 million in net outflows year to date.

Analysts say Texas's blue wave in particular could result in slowed development in the state replete with bitcoin mining facilities and data centers.

Cryptocurrency liquidations also exceeded $1 billion during Sunday’s volatility on 8 November, according to crypto.news.
A reversal in ETF flows would likely require stabilisation in Bitcoin’s spot price and a shift in the macro environment that has weighed on risk assets.
Whether the IBIT-concentrated outflows represent tactical rebalancing by a handful of large holders or the start of a broader redemption cycle will become clearer in the sessions ahead.

Hilbert Group’s Russell Thompson has warned that Bitcoin could fall toward $65,000 if key support breaks, as losses in AI and chip stocks threaten to force investors to sell crypto to meet margin calls.
- Thompson expects Bitcoin selling during deleveraging, followed by a possible return of capital from AI.
- Bitcoin support around $71,900 is central to his conditional warning of a decline toward $65,000.

2, while options pricing favors downside protection.

10, ahead of December’s Fed decision.
Hilbert Group’s chief investment officer, in comments shared with crypto.news on Nov.
9, said funding concerns surrounding smaller AI and semiconductor companies could bring further losses across investment portfolios.
Although he expects some money to return to digital assets eventually, his immediate assessment remains bearish.
“If you start getting margin calls, then you start selling bits of your portfolio that are not particularly core, and that usually means Bitcoin.”
He described “blood in the water” around the AI trade, warning that investment funds exposed to the sector could face further strain.
Bitcoin’s $71,900 support separates two downside scenarios
With Bitcoin trading around $74,200 at the time of his assessment, Thompson identified initial support at $72,800, near the middle of April’s breakout range.
Moving average support sits just below, around $72,700, followed by a larger trend line near $71,900.
He expects buyers below the prevailing price, but said losing the trend line would make $65,000 a concern.
Although $70,000 is an obvious round-number threshold, he sees little technical support there beyond its psychological appeal.
Measured against his $74,200 reference price, a move to $71,900 would represent a decline of approximately 3.1%.
Reaching $65,000 would mean a 12.4% drop.
His caution follows a recovery that failed to hold last week.
Bitcoin climbed above $80,000 on Nov.
5, when the previous session’s $74.6 million in U.S.
spot ETF inflows and heavy short liquidations supported buying.
By Nov.
6, it was back near $76,000 after technology-stock losses and $430.2 million in ETF withdrawals during Thursday’s session.
AI capital could return after forced selling passes
Thompson traces Bitcoin’s earlier peak to investors moving money out of crypto and into chips, AI and technology stocks.
With those trades now losing capital, he believes digital assets could eventually receive some of the money coming out.
His expectation depends on the current deleveraging ending and financial markets settling.
He has not ruled out a Bitcoin breakout before year-end, even as he expects difficult trading in the immediate period.
“Once this period of deleveraging passes and markets calm down, I think some of that capital is likely to flow back.”
The inflation backdrop forms part of his argument for renewed crypto investment, although he still expects forced portfolio selling to weigh on Bitcoin before that potential recovery.
Institutional flows have remained weak.
He estimated Bitcoin ETF withdrawals at $1.2 billion last week.
Separately, the Nov.
8 weekly market coverage recorded $1.28 billion in withdrawals for Nov.
2–6, citing Farside Investors.
Options traders continue paying more for downside protection, according to Thompson.
He put five-delta put implied volatility at 51, compared with 38 for at-the-money options, leaving a 13-point premium.
Comparable calls carried only a one-point premium.
Hilbert’s five-factor global liquidity model has fallen to 2.61, while its six-factor model stands at 3.02.
Thompson describes readings below one as crisis liquidity and readings above nine as abundant liquidity.
The firm’s Nov.
2 update had put those models at 3.23 and 3.27, respectively.
The latest readings are lower by 0.62 and 0.25 points.
CPI arrives as Thompson sees December hike risk
On monetary policy, Thompson said stronger U.S.
employment and wage data had pushed the December Fed meeting into play.
He cited market pricing of a 77% probability of a rate hike and said two hikes between now and next year were the favored outcome.
Yet he sees a counterweight in inflation expectations, which he described as well anchored, alongside lower breakeven rates.
In his assessment, expectations about future inflation could restrain the Fed even when recent economic releases look strong.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics has scheduled October CPI for Tuesday, Nov.
10, at 8:30 a.m.
Eastern Time.
September’s official inflation data showed headline consumer prices rising 0.6% month over month and 3.7% annually.
Excluding food and energy, prices rose 0.3% during the month and 2.6% over the year.

6 placed Bitcoin near $75,799, with its daily relative strength index at 37.82.
Its weekly candle had reached $81,196 before retreating, while the daily price remained below the middle Bollinger band near $79,759.
The latest CoinGlass snapshot shows price below that Nov.
6 reading.
Rebounds during the intervening sessions failed to recover $80,000, leaving the weekly chart with a succession of lower trading ranges.
Channel breakdown brings a $65,000 warning
In a Nov.
11 post, pseudonymous analyst Tranquility Crypto said Bitcoin had traded inside a descending channel since September.
Their chart shows repeated rejections along its upper boundary before price slips beneath the lower trendline.
The analyst described an “expected move coming towards $65K” and said they wanted Bitcoin to reclaim the broken structure before becoming comfortable calling a bottom.
From a $73,500 reference price, reaching $65,000 would mean a further decline of approximately 11.6%.
The screenshot presents the target as a projected move beneath the latest candles, with the channel recovery still absent from the displayed setup.
Short liquidations offer a possible rebound route
In a Nov.
11 X post, analyst Ted Pillows identified a large short-side liquidity cluster between $76,000 and $77,500.
He suggested Bitcoin could rally toward the zone if stocks developed stronger upward momentum.
The one-week CoinGlass heatmap shows bright overhead bands across roughly the same region, with further concentrations around $79,000 and above $81,000.
Smaller bands sit below the latest price around $72,000–$73,000.
Measured from $73,500, reaching $76,000 would require a gain of 3.4%, while $77,500 would require approximately 5.4%.
Both prices remain below the levels traded near the beginning of the weekly chart.
Glassnode says most nearby long-liquidation levels have been cleared.
Its six-month map instead places the largest downside cluster at $59,500–$62,600 and the largest overhead cluster near $87,500.
ETF withdrawals slow while stablecoin supply contracts
As crypto.news previously reported, weekly withdrawals from U.S.
spot Bitcoin ETFs reached approximately $1.28 billion during Nov.
2–6.
BlackRock’s IBIT accounted for $1.21 billion, while Fidelity’s FBTC attracted $93.1 million.
Farside Investors recorded another $201 million leaving the products on Nov.
9 and $95 million on Nov.
10.
Tuesday’s withdrawal was approximately 52.7% smaller than Monday’s, but the daily category totals across Nov.
2–10 still sum to $1.58 billion in net outflows.
IBIT lost $78.2 million on Tuesday, and FBTC shed $36.8 million.
Morgan Stanley’s MSBT received $20 million, partially offsetting those withdrawals.
Glassnode reports a $14.2 billion contraction in stablecoin supply over 30 days through Nov.
9.
Wallet groups holding 100–1,000 BTC and 1,000–10,000 BTC have begun accumulating, although other groups continue reducing balances.
October inflation follows the initial weekly decline
The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Nov.
10 that October consumer prices rose 0.4%, following September’s 0.6% gain.
Core prices rose 0.3% for a third consecutive month.
Subsequent market coverage, citing CoinGlass, reported $723.37 million in crypto liquidations over its 24-hour window, including roughly $570 million in longs.
Bitcoin accounted for approximately $203 million, comprising $175 million in longs and $28 million in shorts.

What is Bitcoin?
Bitcoin is the first cryptocurrency ever created and is still the most widely recognized digital coin available in 2026.
Its market capitalization sits around $1.33 trillion, far above runner-up Ethereum, which has a market value of roughly $233 billion.
At its core, Bitcoin is a decentralized digital currency.
That means it operates on a peer-to-peer network instead of being controlled by a government, bank, or other central authority.
It lets you transfer value straight to another person without using a financial middleman.
Many investors are drawn to Bitcoin because they see it as a potential hedge against inflation or simply as a way to add another asset class to their portfolio.
Over the past decade, its performance has been massive, often beating the returns of major stock market indices, which helps explain why it has captured so much attention.
However, like other cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin is exposed to extreme volatility and can experience rapid price swings.
Bitcoin price history
Since launching in 2009, Bitcoin’s journey has been anything but smooth.
In the early days, software developer and early believer Laszlo Hanyecz famously spent 10,000 Bitcoins on a couple of pizzas; at the time of this writing, those coins would be worth more than $668 million.
Over roughly the last decade, Bitcoin’s price has soared by more than 15,000%.
That upside has come with serious risk, as cryptocurrencies tend to be highly unpredictable.
Bitcoin has experienced steep drops, at times losing tens of thousands of dollars in value within a few months, but it has also staged similarly dramatic rallies.
In 2025, it ended the calendar year about 30% below the all-time high it hit in October of that same year.
What affects Bitcoin’s price?
Several forces can influence the price of Bitcoin, including:
- Investor speculation: As with many assets, trader sentiment and hype play a major role in Bitcoin’s value.
In the short term, its demand often reflects investor instincts and speculative trading activity rather than deeper fundamentals.
- Adoption by major companies: As businesses adopt crypto technology and begin accepting Bitcoin as payment, its growth potential can increase.
For instance, Bitcoin’s price climbed following announcements from companies like Tesla and Ferrari that they would accept it for certain purchases.
- Economy: Bitcoin doesn’t react to inflation data or Federal Reserve decisions in quite the same way as traditional investments such as stocks.
Even so, it often performs better when the U.S.
economy is strong.
When consumers feel flush, they may be more willing to experiment with alternatives like crypto.
- Regulatory developments: Cryptocurrency is still a relatively young space, and regulation is evolving.
New rules or government actions can make investors nervous and affect Bitcoin’s price.
How to buy and invest in Bitcoin
You have several ways to gain exposure to Bitcoin.
Here are some of the most common.
Buy Bitcoin on a cryptocurrency exchange
One of the most straightforward strategies is to buy Bitcoin directly.
You can open an account with a cryptocurrency exchange, connect it to your bank account, and then use your funds to purchase Bitcoin.
Invest in Bitcoin ETFs
If you prefer not to hold Bitcoin yourself, you might consider a cryptocurrency exchange-traded fund (ETF).
A Bitcoin ETF owns Bitcoin on your behalf, and its shares trade on regular stock exchanges.
This approach lets you avoid setting up a separate crypto wallet and lowers the risk of losing access to your coins due to password or wallet mishaps.
Buy crypto stocks
Investors who are hesitant to invest in Bitcoin directly can also look at stocks tied to the crypto industry.
These may include technology companies, publicly traded crypto exchanges, or payment processors.
Because these businesses use or hold Bitcoin in their operations, their performance can be influenced by Bitcoin’s price, giving you indirect exposure.
Open a Bitcoin IRA
For those focused on retirement, a Bitcoin IRA might be appealing.
It’s a tax-advantaged retirement account that lets you use your retirement contributions to buy Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies.
A Bitcoin IRA offers the same tax benefits and contribution limits as traditional or Roth IRAs, but it allows you to invest in alternative assets.
Bitcoin vs.

While Bitcoin is the best-known name in crypto, it’s not your only choice.

Bitcoin ETFs flip negative for 2026 after $1.28 billion outflow week, worst since June
The 12 U.S.-listed spot bitcoin funds have now lost $914.1 million for the year, while ether, Solana and Hyperliquid ETFs all extended weekly outflow streaks in a brutal turn for crypto ETFs.
Quick Take
- U.S.
spot bitcoin ETFs saw $1.28 billion in net outflows last week, their worst weekly sum since late June.
- The outflows left bitcoin ETFs with about $914.1 million in net outflows for 2026, reversing their year-to-date gains.
- BlackRock’s IBIT accounted for 88% of Friday’s gross outflows, with $403 million leaving the industry-leading fund.
- Spot ether ETFs lost $365.3 million, their sixth consecutive negative week.
- Solana and Hyperliquid ETFs each logged a fifth straight week of outflows, the longest streaks for both types of funds since they each began trading.
U.S.
spot bitcoin ETFs logged $1.28 billion in net outflows last week, their worst week since late June, per The Block's analysis of SoSoValue data.
It was the funds' second straight negative week and made the top ten largest weekly outflows since they launched in January 2024 at #7.
The funds saw outflows every day except Wednesday last week, per the data.
They lost $398.6 million on Monday, $115.6 million on Tuesday, $430.2 million on Thursday and $411.9 million on Friday, with Wednesday's relatively modest $74.6 million inflow marking the only positive day.
The most recent worse week ended June 26, when the funds shed $1.79 billion in what The Block reported at the time was their second-worst week on record.
Bitcoin ETFs lost $202.6 million the week before last, including a $643.3 million Friday outflow that was the largest single-day exit in four months after the record Binance hack.
BlackRock's IBIT accounted for $403 million of Friday's loss, or about 88% of the day's gross outflows.
Bitwise's BITB and Ark & 21Shares' ARKB each lost about $20 million, and Grayscale's GBTC shed $11.1 million.
Fidelity's FBTC took in $42.8 million on Friday, after leading Thursday's outflows with $199.9 million, as The Block reported.
Bitcoin funds turn negative for 2026
The week's outflows erased bitcoin ETFs' gains for the year.
The funds entered the week with about $368 million in 2026 net inflows, after turning positive for the year in late September.
Monday's outflows pushed that figure below zero, and the funds closed Friday at about $914.1 million in net outflows year to date.
The total value of bitcoin held across the 12 funds dropped 2.3% to $95.9 billion, equal to about 6.3% of the cryptocurrency's market capitalization.
IBIT held $60.3 billion in net assets against $65.1 billion in cumulative inflows.
The outflows came amid a crypto and equities selloff after Tuesday's midterm elections.
Bitcoin fell 5.6% on Thursday alone, and analysts linked the slide to the Democratic sweep of Congress and doubts over AI spending, The Block reported Friday.
Analysts say Texas's blue wave in particular could result in slowed development in the state replete with bitcoin mining facilities and data centers.
Ether funds extend losing run to six weeks
Spot ether ETFs lost $365.3 million last week, per SoSoValue data, their sixth straight week of net outflows.
The run has drained about $2.02 billion from the funds since late September.
Ether ETFs have twice posted eight-week losing streaks, most recently when they matched that record in early July.
Like the bitcoin funds, ether ETFs had only one positive trading day last week, also on Wednesday, when they gained $53 million.
Monday's $139.8 million outflow was the week's largest, followed by $100 million on Thursday and $93.2 million on Friday.
BlackRock's ETHA accounted for $90.8 million of Friday's total, about 96% of the gross losses, mirroring the firm's bitcoin fund.
The products are now down about $405.6 million for 2026.
Net assets fell 2.9% over the week to $12.84 billion, against $11.92 billion in cumulative net inflows.
Solana, Hyperliquid funds post longest outflow runs
Spot Solana ETFs lost $26.3 million last week, per SoSoValue, nearly all of it on Friday.
It was their fifth straight negative week, the longest streak since the funds launched in October 2025, and brought five-week outflows to $165.4 million.
The streak began the week the funds ended a record 14-week inflow run.
Bitwise's BSOL led Friday's Solana outflows with $14.4 million, followed by Grayscale's GSOL at $5.4 million.
The funds held $1.31 billion in net assets as of Friday, down from $1.40 billion a week earlier, though they remain about $676.2 million positive for the year.
The three publicly traded Hyperliquid ETFs shed $15.6 million, also extending their outflow streak to five weeks, the longest since they began trading in May.
The funds have lost $58.4 million over that stretch, and their net assets fell about 17% on the week to $374.1 million.
Friday's $8 million outflow was led by Bitwise's BHYP.
Bitcoin traded near $75,880 on Saturday morning, while ether changed hands around $2,244, SOL near $89.84 and HYPE around $77.79, according to The Block's price pages.

Bitcoin (BTC) returned above $75,000 after Monday’s Wall Street open as tech stocks rebounded.
Key points:
- Bitcoin bounced from 11-week lows of $73,500 on Monday as investors added tech-stock exposure.
- Stock markets moved beyond controversy surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, with the Nasdaq Composite Index gaining up to 2.6% on Monday.
- BTC price analysis saw the potential for a dip toward the 200-week simple moving average trend line at $67,755.
Bitcoin, stocks shake off Nvidia jitters

The weakness accompanied news that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang may have been the target of a Chinese intelligence effort, a claim Beijing subsequently denied.
Nvidia stock fell about 6% to $170.24 on Monday early trading, a level it last traded at on March 31, before rebounding to session highs of $179.92.

In a Sunday note, Dan Ives, senior managing director at merchant bank Yorkville Ives & Co., warned that the episode could create lasting headwinds for Nvidia’s share price.

Gary Gensler, former chair of the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), said that Nvidia’s board would face “tough choices” based on the results of the company’s internal investigation.
Elsewhere, investors sought to buy the lows on tech stocks, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index shaking off the Nvidia claims to gain 2.5% in the first hour of the US trading session.

At 6:30 a.m.
Eastern Time today, the going rate for one Bitcoin (BTC) is $73,208.24.
That’s $729.54 lower than yesterday morning’s level and about $28,420 below where it stood a year ago.
What is Bitcoin?
Bitcoin holds the distinction of being the original cryptocurrency and remains the most widely followed digital coin today.
Its market capitalization is around $1.33 trillion, putting it well ahead of Ethereum—the second-largest cryptocurrency—which has about $233 billion in market value.
Put simply, Bitcoin is a decentralized digital currency.
Rather than being issued or managed by a central bank or government, it runs on a peer-to-peer network.
That setup enables people to send money directly to one another without going through a traditional financial institution.
Many investors view Bitcoin as a possible shield against inflation or as another tool for diversifying their portfolios.
Its growth over the last decade has been remarkable, frequently beating the performance of major stock market indices, which has helped fuel investors’ interest.
However, like most cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin is known for sharp volatility and rapid changes in price.
Bitcoin price history
Since its creation in 2009, Bitcoin’s price action has been anything but boring.
One of the most famous early stories involves software developer Laszlo Hanyecz, who paid 10,000 Bitcoins for pizza; those coins would now be worth more than 668 million dollars.
Over roughly the past decade, Bitcoin has gained more than 15,000%.
That’s an extraordinary rise by any measure.
Yet this performance comes with substantial risk, as cryptocurrencies can be extremely unpredictable.
Bitcoin has endured steep corrections, with declines of tens of thousands of dollars over short periods, but it has also rebounded with powerful rallies.
By the end of 2025, it was trading about 30% below its record high from October of the same year.
What affects Bitcoin’s price?
A number of elements can move Bitcoin’s price, including:
- Investor speculation: As with many high-risk assets, Bitcoin is heavily influenced by what traders think and feel.
Short-term price changes often reflect speculative bets and market buzz more than long-term fundamentals.
- Adoption by major companies: When large, well-known companies embrace Bitcoin or crypto technology, it can support further growth.
For instance, Bitcoin experienced price increases after automakers like Tesla and Ferrari revealed plans to accept Bitcoin as a form of payment.
- Economy: Bitcoin doesn’t respond to inflation reports or Federal Reserve decisions in the same way as more traditional assets like stocks.
Still, it tends to do better when the U.S.
economy is strong, as people with more disposable income may be open to investing in higher-risk assets like crypto.
- Regulatory developments: Because the crypto space is still maturing, rules and regulations are still being developed.
New regulatory actions can unsettle the market and impact Bitcoin’s price, either positively or negatively.
How to buy and invest in Bitcoin
If you’re interested in adding Bitcoin to your portfolio, you have several choices.
Here are some popular ones.
Buy Bitcoin on a cryptocurrency exchange
One direct method is to buy Bitcoin yourself.
This involves opening an account with a cryptocurrency exchange, linking it to your bank, and using your deposited funds to purchase Bitcoin.
Invest in Bitcoin ETFs
If you’d rather not handle crypto directly, you can look at Bitcoin exchange-traded funds.
A Bitcoin ETF holds Bitcoin as its underlying asset, and the fund’s shares trade on regular stock exchanges.
This route lets you avoid managing your own crypto wallet and lowers the risk of losing access to your coins through lost passwords or wallet errors.
Buy crypto stocks
Another investment strategy is to buy shares of companies that are deeply involved in crypto.
These might include tech companies, publicly traded crypto exchanges, or payment processors that integrate Bitcoin.
When these businesses benefit from Bitcoin’s success, their stocks may respond, giving you indirect exposure.
Open a Bitcoin IRA
Retirement savers may consider a Bitcoin IRA.
This type of account works similarly to a traditional or Roth IRA in that it offers tax advantages and the same contribution limits, but it allows you to invest in Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies as part of your retirement strategy.
Bitcoin vs.
other cryptocurrencies
Even though Bitcoin gets much of the attention, it’s just one of many cryptocurrencies to consider.
When choosing where to invest, it may also be worth evaluating the following.
- Ethereum: Ethereum is the second-biggest cryptocurrency by market cap.
In contrast to Bitcoin, its primary function is not as a currency but as a decentralized platform that powers applications and smart contracts, making it especially popular among developers.
- Tether: Tether is classified as a “stablecoin” because it is pegged to another asset—in this case, the U.S.
dollar.
As a result, it tends to be less volatile than Bitcoin, though it also offers less potential for big gains.
- XRP: XRP is built for fast and inexpensive cross-border payments, allowing money to move between countries quickly and with relatively low fees.

Is it a good time to invest in Bitcoin?
By the standards of long-established blue-chip companies like Walmart, Procter & Gamble, and Coca-Cola, Bitcoin is still fairly young.
That makes it challenging to predict how it will behave far into the future.
Even so, its recent performance has been strong.
As merchants and corporations begin accepting Bitcoin for payments, its price may have room to climb—and as it matures, it could see somewhat less extreme volatility.
That said, you should avoid treating Bitcoin as a sure thing.
Only invest money you won’t need soon, and maintain a diversified portfolio so other assets can help balance any large moves in Bitcoin’s price.
For many people, Bitcoin is best viewed as a long-term, higher-risk holding rather than a short-term speculation.
It may not suit you if you cannot tolerate big price swings.
But if you’re willing to hold through volatility and keep Bitcoin as one component of a diversified portfolio, allocating a portion of your money to it may make sense.
Frequently asked questions
How much will Bitcoin be worth in 2030?
While the answer is obviously unknowable, crypto experts are generally optimistic about the short-term success of Bitcoin.
Some models price it at more than $700,000 by 2030, with conservative estimates closer to $300,000.
What is Bitcoin’s all-time high price?
As of this writing, Bitcoin reached its highest price ever on Oct.
6, 2025, pricing at a whopping $126,198.07.
Can you buy a fraction of a Bitcoin?
Yes, you can buy a fraction of a Bitcoin.
Most cryptocurrency exchanges offer fractional investing, meaning you can buy portions of crypto coins.
Thanks to fractional investing, you can invest in Bitcoin with as little as a few dollars.
How do I start investing in Bitcoin as a beginner?
If you want to invest directly in Bitcoin by owning the currency, you’ll typically open an account with a cryptocurrency exchange.
Once the account is created, you can transfer money to your crypto account from your bank and place an order for Bitcoin and other tokens or coins.
You can also indirectly invest in Bitcoin via an ETF or a business that uses Bitcoin.
What can you buy with Bitcoin?
You can use your Bitcoin holdings in several ways, from selling for cash to trading it for other coins.
In some cases, you can also pay for purchases, such as with Tesla and Microsoft.
